igcse-0580-trigonometry-pythagoras.description: Identify the hypotenuse and use Pythagoras to find either a missing side or a diagonal.

sections.title: How do I identify and find the hypotenuse?
sections.label: Find the side opposite 90°
sections.intro: Find the square corner first. The side across from that angle is the hypotenuse and is always the longest side.

blocks.html: For perpendicular legs \(a,b\) and hypotenuse \(c\), use \(c^2=a^2+b^2\). If you know \(c\), write \(a=\sqrt{c^2-b^2}\) to find the missing leg.

figure.alt: Triangle ABC has its right angle at B. AC is its longest side. AB and BC are its perpendicular legs.
figure.caption: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, even when the triangle is turned.

blocks.title: Find the hypotenuse
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(AB=4\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(BC=8\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Calculate \(AC\) in exact form.
blocks.solution:
AC is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle.

\(AC^2=4^2+8^2=80\)

\(AC=\sqrt{80}=4 \sqrt{5}\)

Answer \(4 \sqrt{5}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: Add the squares of the two legs. Take the positive square root at the end.

blocks.html: Add the squared legs to find the hypotenuse. Subtract a leg's square from the hypotenuse square to find a leg.

blocks.title: Find the shorter side
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(AB=5\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(AC=16\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(BC\) exactly.
blocks.solution:
The given hypotenuse is AC.

\(BC^2=16^2-5^2=231\)

\(BC=\sqrt{231}\)

Answer \(\sqrt{231}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the square of the known leg from the square of the hypotenuse.

blocks.html: Label the hypotenuse before substituting.

sections.title: Where is the right triangle hiding?
sections.label: Sketch a right-angled corner
sections.intro: A rectangle and many route problems contain a right angle even when no triangle is drawn.

blocks.html: Draw the diagonal to make a triangle. When all three side lengths are known, compare the square of the longest side with the sum of the other squares.

blocks.title: Find the diagonal of a rectangle
blocks.prompt: A rectangular panel has edges \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find its diagonal to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
A diagonal and the two adjacent edges make a right-angled triangle.

\(d^2=8^2+6^2=100\)

\(d=\sqrt{100}\)

Answer \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Use the corner of the rectangle as the right angle.

blocks.html: Three whole-number lengths do not guarantee a right angle.

blocks.title: Test whether an angle is a right angle
blocks.prompt: A sample of rods has lengths \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(29\,\mathrm{cm}\). Can these be the three sides of a right-angled triangle?

options.A: No, the squares do not balance.
options.B: Yes, every set of three integer lengths is right-angled.
options.C: It cannot be decided from the side lengths.

blocks.solution:
The only possible hypotenuse is the longest rod.

\(15^2+20^2=625\)

\(29^2=841\)

The values differ.

Answer No, the squares do not balance..
blocks.hint: Compare the square of the longest side with the sum of the other squares.

blocks.html: Write one equation that shows the comparison or the mark for the right angle.

sections.title: How should I finish a length calculation?
sections.label: Take the positive root
sections.intro: The theorem relates squares. A question asking for a length expects the positive square root of the result.

blocks.html: Leave the root exact when asked. Otherwise work with the full calculator result and round at the end.

blocks.title: Recover a rectangle edge from its diagonal
blocks.prompt: A rectangular banner is \(83\,\mathrm{cm}\) across its diagonal and \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\) along one edge. Find the length of the other edge to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
Treat the diagonal as the hypotenuse.

\(w^2=83^2-18^2=6565\)

\(w=\sqrt{6565}\)

Answer \(81\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Choose subtraction because the diagonal is already known.

blocks.html: Rounding a diagonal before reusing it can change the final answer.

blocks.title: Check the length of an L-shaped route shortcut
blocks.prompt: A machine travels \(45\,\mathrm{cm}\) north and then \(40\,\mathrm{cm}\) east. Calculate the exact straight-line distance from start to finish.
blocks.solution:
North and east are perpendicular.

\(d^2=45^2+40^2=3625\)

\(d=5 \sqrt{145}\)

Answer \(5 \sqrt{145}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: Use the straight-line distance across the right angle.

blocks.html: Check whether the length ought to be larger or smaller than the known side.

igcse-0580-trigonometry-right-triangle-r.description: Use sine, cosine and tangent to find an acute angle or missing side in a right-angled triangle.

sections.title: Which two sides does each ratio use?
sections.label: Label sides from the reference angle
sections.intro: Start at the marked acute angle. The opposite side is across from it. The adjacent leg touches it. The hypotenuse is across from the right angle.

blocks.html: \(\sin\theta=\frac{\rm opposite}{\rm hypotenuse}\), \(\cos\theta=\frac{\rm adjacent}{\rm hypotenuse}\) and \(\tan\theta=\frac{\rm opposite}{\rm adjacent}\).

figure.alt: In triangle ABC the right angle is at B and the reference angle is A. BC is opposite A, AB is adjacent and AC is the hypotenuse.
figure.caption: Opposite and adjacent depend on the reference angle. The hypotenuse is fixed.

blocks.title: Use sine to find the opposite side
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(A=49^\circ\) and \(AC=8\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Calculate \(BC\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
Use opposite and hypotenuse.

\(\sin 49^\circ=\frac{BC}{8}\)

\(BC=8\times \sin 49^\circ\)

Answer \(6.04\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Label the sides relative to angle A before choosing the ratio.

blocks.html: Changing the reference angle changes the opposite and adjacent labels.

blocks.title: Find the adjacent leg with cosine
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(AC=13\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(A=48^\circ\).

Find \(AB\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
AB touches A and is not opposite the right angle.

\(\cos 48^\circ=\frac{AB}{13}\)

\(AB=13\cos 48^\circ\)

Answer \(8.7\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: The leg that touches A is adjacent.

blocks.html: The ratio that uses the known and requested sides is the one to choose.

sections.title: When do I multiply or divide?
sections.label: Rearrange before calculating
sections.intro: For a side on top of the fraction, multiply by the denominator. For a side below the fraction, isolate it first.

blocks.html: For example, if \(\cos 38^\circ=\frac{7}{h}\), then \(h=\frac{7}{\cos 38^\circ}\).

blocks.title: Use tangent to find the opposite side
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(A=55^\circ\) and \(AB=9\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Calculate \(BC\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
Use opposite and adjacent.

\(\tan 55^\circ=\frac{BC}{9}\)

\(BC=9\times \tan 55^\circ\)

Answer \(12.9\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Label the sides relative to angle A before choosing the ratio.

blocks.html: Multiplying by the cosine would make the hypotenuse shorter than a leg.

blocks.title: Use cosine to find the hypotenuse
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(A=58^\circ\) and \(AB=9\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Calculate \(AC\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
Use adjacent and hypotenuse.

\(\cos 58^\circ=\frac{9}{AC}\)

\(AC=\frac{9}{\cos 58^\circ}\)

Answer \(17\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Label the sides relative to angle A before choosing the ratio.

blocks.html: Compare the relative sizes of the sides in your answer.

sections.title: How can I find a missing acute angle?
sections.label: Use the inverse key in degree mode
sections.intro: Choose the ratio using the two known sides. The calculator's inverse key gives the angle from the ratio.

blocks.html: For \(\tan\theta=\frac{5}{9}\), enter \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac59\right)\) in degree mode.

blocks.title: Find an acute angle using inverse cos
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(AB=7\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(AC=14\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Calculate \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
\(\cos A=\frac{7}{14}\)

Use inverse cos in degree mode.

\(A=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{7}{14}\right)\)

Answer \(60.0^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Use the inverse key for the ratio, as the unknown is an angle.

blocks.html: Inverse tangent gives an angle. Taking the reciprocal of the fraction does something different.

blocks.title: Find an acute angle using inverse tan
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(BC=8\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(AB=14\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Calculate \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
\(\tan A=\frac{8}{14}\)

Use inverse tan in degree mode.

\(A=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{14}\right)\)

Answer \(29.7^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Use the inverse key for the ratio, as the unknown is an angle.

blocks.html: For an angle given as a decimal, use one decimal place unless the question sets another precision.

igcse-0580-trigonometry-bearings-and-two.description: Draw a route, combine perpendicular displacements and calculate clockwise three-figure bearings.

sections.title: How do I read or reverse a bearing?
sections.label: Draw north at the departure point
sections.intro: A bearing is measured clockwise from north at the starting point. ‘The bearing of B from A’ starts at A.

blocks.html: To reverse a bearing add or subtract \(180^\circ\) and give the value in a single turn, with leading zeroes where needed.

figure.alt: An arrow from A points north. The route AB lies east of north. The clockwise angle from the north line to AB is marked.
figure.caption: Start at the north line through the departure point, then turn clockwise to the direction of travel.

blocks.title: Reverse a three-figure bearing
blocks.prompt: The bearing of \(Q\) from \(P\) is \(323^\circ\). Find the bearing of \(P\) from \(Q\).
blocks.solution:
The north lines are parallel. Reversing direction adds 180В° before reducing to a full turn.

\(b=323^\circ+180^\circ\)

Use the remaining angle within a full turn.

Answer \(143^\circ\).
blocks.hint: The direction reverses by half of a turn.

blocks.html: Using a north line at the destination gives the reverse direction.

blocks.title: Use a right triangle to calculate a bearing
blocks.prompt: \(B\) is \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\) east and \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\) north of \(A\). Find the bearing of \(B\) from \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
Start at the north line through A. The smaller angle is opposite the east displacement.

\(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{9}\right)\)

Read this from north clockwise.

\(b=\alpha\)

Answer \(029.1^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Measure from north clockwise, with the north line at the starting point.

blocks.html: Write a whole-degree bearing with three figures, for example \(072^\circ\).

sections.title: How do I get a bearing from a right triangle?
sections.label: Find the small angle and convert it
sections.intro: Sketch horizontal east–west and vertical north–south displacements. The line from departure to arrival gives the bearing.

blocks.html: Use inverse tangent to find the small angle from north for northward travel. For northwest directions, subtract that small angle from \(360^\circ\).

blocks.title: Use a right triangle to calculate a bearing
blocks.prompt: \(B\) is \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) west and \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\) north of \(A\). Find the bearing of \(B\) from \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
Start at the north line through A. The smaller angle is opposite the west displacement.

\(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{9}\right)\)

The direction is west of north. Subtract the smaller angle from a full turn.

\(b=360^\circ-\alpha\)

Answer \(326.3^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Measure from north clockwise, with the north line at the starting point.

blocks.html: A northwest direction has a bearing between \(270^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\), even though the computed triangle angle is acute.

blocks.title: Find the direct distance after a right-angle turn
blocks.prompt: A delivery robot travels \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\) due east and then \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\) due south. Find the exact distance back to its starting point.
blocks.solution:
An eastward move and a southward move are perpendicular.

\(d^2=7^2+9^2\)

\(d=\sqrt{130}\)

Answer \(\sqrt{130}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: The direct route is the hypotenuse of the journey triangle.

blocks.html: Check the quadrant before deciding whether to use a small angle as it stands.

sections.title: Which calculation gives the direct distance or a displacement?
sections.label: Match the target to the sketch
sections.intro: Perpendicular trips make the legs of the route triangle. An inclined route can also be the hypotenuse of a triangle of displacements.

blocks.html: Use Pythagoras for the straight distance from two perpendicular trips. Use sine or cosine to turn a known route and bearing into one component.

blocks.title: Resolve an eastward displacement
blocks.prompt: A model boat travels \(16\,\mathrm{cm}\) on a bearing of \(052^\circ\). Find its eastward displacement to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
The given bearing is the angle from the northward leg to the route. The eastward displacement is opposite.

\(e=16\sin 52^\circ\)

Answer \(12.6\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Sketch north and east through the departure point.

blocks.html: The length of the travelled route is the sum of its legs. The straight-line distance is the hypotenuse.

blocks.title: Read the right triangle in a 2D plan
blocks.prompt: A diagonal shortcut crosses a rectangle of horizontal width \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\) and vertical width \(11\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the acute angle between the shortcut and its horizontal side to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
The vertical side is opposite the angle at the horizontal side.

\(\tan \theta=\frac{11}{18}\)

\(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{11}{18}\right)\)

Answer \(31.4^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Find the acute angle with the horizontal side; use the two perpendicular widths.

blocks.html: Check that the direct distance is shorter than the sum of the two legs.

examples.question: A delivery robot travels \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\) due east and then \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) due south. Find the exact distance back to its starting point.
solution: An eastward move and a southward move are perpendicular.

examples.title: Resolve an eastward displacement
examples.question: A model boat travels \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\) on a bearing of \(033^\circ\). Find its eastward displacement to 3 significant figures.
solution: The given bearing is the angle from the northward leg to the route. The eastward displacement is opposite.

examples.title: Read the right triangle in a 2D plan
examples.question: A diagonal shortcut crosses a rectangle of horizontal width \(14\,\mathrm{cm}\) and vertical width \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the acute angle between the shortcut and its horizontal side to 1 decimal place.
solution: The vertical side is opposite the angle at the horizontal side.

extraPractice.title: Reverse a three-figure bearing
extraPractice.prompt: The bearing of \(Q\) from \(P\) is \(340^\circ\). Find the bearing of \(P\) from \(Q\).
extraPractice.solution:
The north lines are parallel. Reversing direction adds 180В° before reducing to a full turn.

\(b=340^\circ+180^\circ\)

Use the remaining angle within a full turn.

Answer \(160^\circ\).
extraPractice.hint: The direction reverses by half of a turn.

extraPractice.title: Use a right triangle to calculate a bearing
extraPractice.prompt: \(B\) is \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) east and \(13\,\mathrm{cm}\) north of \(A\). Find the bearing of \(B\) from \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
Start at the north line through A. The smaller angle is opposite the east displacement.

\(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{13}\right)\)

Read this from north clockwise.

\(b=\alpha\)

Answer \(024.8^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Measure from north clockwise, with the north line at the starting point.

extraPractice.title: Use a right triangle to calculate a bearing
extraPractice.prompt: \(B\) is \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\) west and \(13\,\mathrm{cm}\) north of \(A\). Find the bearing of \(B\) from \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
Start at the north line through A. The smaller angle is opposite the west displacement.

\(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{7}{13}\right)\)

The direction is west of north. Subtract the smaller angle from a full turn.

\(b=360^\circ-\alpha\)

Answer \(331.7^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Measure from north clockwise, with the north line at the starting point.

extraPractice.title: Find the direct distance after a right-angle turn
extraPractice.prompt: A delivery robot travels \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) due east and then \(13\,\mathrm{cm}\) due south. Find the exact distance back to its starting point.
extraPractice.solution:
An eastward move and a southward move are perpendicular.

\(d^2=8^2+13^2\)

\(d=\sqrt{233}\)

Answer \(\sqrt{233}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
extraPractice.hint: The direct route is the hypotenuse of the journey triangle.

extraPractice.title: Resolve an eastward displacement
extraPractice.prompt: A model boat travels \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\) on a bearing of \(044^\circ\). Find its eastward displacement to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.solution:
The given bearing is the angle from the northward leg to the route. The eastward displacement is opposite.

\(e=18\sin 44^\circ\)

Answer \(12.5\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: Sketch north and east through the departure point.

extraPractice.title: Read the right triangle in a 2D plan
extraPractice.prompt: A diagonal shortcut crosses a rectangle of horizontal width \(22\,\mathrm{cm}\) and vertical width \(16\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the acute angle between the shortcut and its horizontal side to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
The vertical side is opposite the angle at the horizontal side.

\(\tan \theta=\frac{16}{22}\)

\(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{16}{22}\right)\)

Answer \(36.0^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Find the acute angle with the horizontal side; use the two perpendicular widths.

glossary.definition: An angle measured clockwise from north at departure.
The change in position along a stated direction.
Exactly east, at the bearing \(090^\circ\).

Methods

Known informationMethod
Draw north at the departure pointTo reverse a bearing add or subtract \(180^\circ\) and give the value in a single turn, with leading zeroes where needed.
Find the small angle and convert itUse inverse tangent to find the small angle from north for northward travel. For northwest directions, subtract that small angle from \(360^\circ\).
Match the target to the sketchUse Pythagoras for the straight distance from two perpendicular trips. Use sine or cosine to turn a known route and bearing into one component.

Worked line

Reverse \(062^\circ\) by adding \(180^\circ\) to get \(242^\circ\).

Check yourself

Reverse the bearing \(305^\circ\).

Answer \(125^\circ\)

• Using a north line at the destination gives the reverse direction.
  • A northwest direction has a bearing between \(270^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\), even though the computed triangle angle is acute.
  • The length of the travelled route is the sum of its legs. The straight-line distance is the hypotenuse.
revision.examTip: Check that the direct distance is shorter than the sum of the two legs.

igcse-0580-trigonometry-elevation-and-di.description: Use a horizontal reference to solve sight-line problems and draw the perpendicular distance to a line.

sections.title: Where is the angle of elevation or depression measured?
sections.label: Draw both horizontal lines
sections.intro: The angle of elevation is measured upwards from the horizontal through the observer. The angle of depression is measured downwards from that horizontal.

blocks.html: If observer and target each have a horizontal line, the angles of elevation and depression between them have the same size.

figure.alt: A slope joins an observer on the left to a target higher on the right. A dashed horizontal through each point shows equal elevation and depression angles.
figure.caption: Each marked angle is measured from a horizontal line. The two horizontal lines are parallel.

blocks.title: Measure an elevation from the horizontal
blocks.prompt: From a point on level ground \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\) from a vertical pole, the angle of elevation to the top is \(52^\circ\). Find the pole height to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
The angle starts at the horizontal through the observer's point on the ground.

\(\tan 52^\circ=\frac{h}{18}\)

\(h=18\tan 52^\circ\)

Answer \(23\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: The height is opposite and the ground distance is adjacent.

blocks.html: The angle from the vertical is the complement, rather than the given elevation or depression.

blocks.title: Measure a depression from the horizontal
blocks.prompt: From the top of a vertical platform \(11\,\mathrm{cm}\) above a level floor, the angle of depression to a marker on the floor is \(59^\circ\). Find the marker's horizontal distance from the base to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal lines through the observer and marker are parallel. The angle of elevation at the marker is also \(59^\circ\).

\(\tan 59^\circ=\frac{11}{d}\)

\(d=\frac{11}{\tan 59^\circ}\)

Answer \(6.61\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: The depression is below the horizontal, not from a vertical edge.

blocks.html: Place the marked angle at the correct observer before choosing a ratio.

sections.title: What makes the shortest distance to a line?
sections.label: Meet the line at 90°
sections.intro: Drop a perpendicular from the point to the line. Every sloping segment from that point to another point on the line would be the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

blocks.html: The perpendicular is shorter than those sloping segments. Use the right triangle with the perpendicular as a leg to calculate its length.

figure.alt: Point P lies above a straight line. PF meets it at ninety degrees. The sloping segment PQ is the hypotenuse.
figure.caption: The length PF is the shortest distance to the line. A sloping route to another point is longer.

blocks.title: Draw the shortest path to a line
blocks.prompt: A straight path passes through \(A\). Point \(P\) is at distance \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\) from \(A\). The acute angle between \(AP\) and the path is \(63^\circ\). Find the shortest distance from \(P\) to the path to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
Drop a perpendicular from P to the straight path. The perpendicular is opposite the given angle.

\(d=15\sin 63^\circ\)

Answer \(13.4\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: The straight route from P to the line meets the line at 90В°.

blocks.html: A line that looks almost vertical in a sketch need not be perpendicular. Mark the right angle.

blocks.title: Compare a direct sloping path with the perpendicular
blocks.prompt: Point \(P\) is \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\) from the foot \(F\) of its perpendicular to a line. Point \(Q\) is \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\) along the line from \(F\). Find the exact length \(PQ\).
blocks.solution:
PFQ is a right-angled triangle. PQ is its hypotenuse and is longer than PF.

\(PQ^2=7^2+12^2\)

\(PQ=\sqrt{193}\)

Answer \(\sqrt{193}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: The perpendicular is one leg of the triangle.

blocks.html: Use ‘from a point to a line’ to identify where an auxiliary right angle is needed.

sections.title: How can the observer's height change the result?
sections.label: Find the vertical difference first
sections.intro: A sight-line triangle starts at the observer's horizontal level. Its vertical leg measures the difference in height between observer and target.

blocks.html: When looking up to a tower, add the observer's height after finding the rise from eye level.

blocks.title: Account for the height of the observer
blocks.prompt: An observer's camera is \(\frac{9}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\) above a level bench. The foot of a vertical model tower is \(19\,\mathrm{cm}\) horizontally away. The angle of elevation from the camera to the top is \(58^\circ\). Find the tower height to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
The right triangle starts at camera level.

\(h_{\text{above camera}}=19\tan 58^\circ\)

\(h_{\text{tower}}=\frac{9}{2}+h_{\text{above camera}}\)

Answer \(34.9\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Add the camera height after finding the rise above it.

blocks.html: The full height is not the opposite side when the observer's eyes are above ground.

blocks.title: Find an angle of depression
blocks.prompt: A small observation camera is \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\) vertically above a flat floor. A target is \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\) horizontally from the point directly below the camera. Find the angle of depression to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
Use the angle from the horizontal along the line of sight.

\(\tan \theta=\frac{12}{20}\)

\(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{12}{20}\right)\)

Answer \(31.0^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: The vertical separation is opposite the angle of elevation at the target.

blocks.html: Mark the horizontal separation and the observer's height as different quantities.

solution: The angle starts at the horizontal through the observer's point on the ground.

solution: PFQ is a right-angled triangle. PQ is its hypotenuse and is longer than PF.

solution: The right triangle starts at camera level.

examples.title: Find an angle of depression
examples.question: A small observation camera is \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) vertically above a flat floor. A target is \(13\,\mathrm{cm}\) horizontally from the point directly below the camera. Find the angle of depression to 1 decimal place.
solution: Use the angle from the horizontal along the line of sight.

extraPractice.title: Measure an elevation from the horizontal
extraPractice.prompt: From a point on level ground \(28\,\mathrm{cm}\) from a vertical pole, the angle of elevation to the top is \(50^\circ\). Find the pole height to 3 significant figures.

extraPractice.solution:
The horizontal lines through the observer and marker are parallel. The angle of elevation at the marker is also \(57^\circ\).

\(\tan 57^\circ=\frac{8}{d}\)

\(d=\frac{8}{\tan 57^\circ}\)

Answer \(5.2\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: The depression is below the horizontal, not from a vertical edge.

extraPractice.title: Draw the shortest path to a line
extraPractice.prompt: A straight path passes through \(A\). Point \(P\) is at distance \(24\,\mathrm{cm}\) from \(A\). The acute angle between \(AP\) and the path is \(32^\circ\). Find the shortest distance from \(P\) to the path to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.solution:
Drop a perpendicular from P to the straight path. The perpendicular is opposite the given angle.

\(d=24\sin 32^\circ\)

Answer \(12.7\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: The straight route from P to the line meets the line at 90В°.

extraPractice.title: Compare a direct sloping path with the perpendicular
extraPractice.prompt: Point \(P\) is \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) from the foot \(F\) of its perpendicular to a line. Point \(Q\) is \(16\,\mathrm{cm}\) along the line from \(F\). Find the exact length \(PQ\).
extraPractice.solution:
PFQ is a right-angled triangle. PQ is its hypotenuse and is longer than PF.

\(PQ^2=8^2+16^2\)

\(PQ=\sqrt{320}\)

Answer \(8 \sqrt{5}\,\mathrm{cm}\).

extraPractice.title: Account for the height of the observer
extraPractice.prompt: An observer's camera is \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\) above a level bench. The foot of a vertical model tower is \(29\,\mathrm{cm}\) horizontally away. The angle of elevation from the camera to the top is \(39^\circ\). Find the tower height to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.solution:
The right triangle starts at camera level.

\(h_{\text{above camera}}=29\tan 39^\circ\)

\(h_{\text{tower}}=5+h_{\text{above camera}}\)

Answer \(28.5\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: Add the camera height after finding the rise above it.

extraPractice.title: Find an angle of depression
extraPractice.prompt: A small observation camera is \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) vertically above a flat floor. A target is \(29\,\mathrm{cm}\) horizontally from the point directly below the camera. Find the angle of depression to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the angle from the horizontal along the line of sight.

\(\tan \theta=\frac{8}{29}\)

\(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{29}\right)\)

Answer \(15.4^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: The vertical separation is opposite the angle of elevation at the target.

sections.title: What are the exact sine and cosine values?
sections.label: Read symmetry and boundary values
sections.intro: Use the special triangles for the interior angles. Sine and cosine trade roles as the angle changes to its complement.

blocks.html: Sine has value 0 at \(0^\circ\) and 1 at \(90^\circ\). Cosine has value 1 at \(0^\circ\) and 0 at \(90^\circ\).

figure.alt: The first right triangle comes from half an equilateral triangle. The other right triangle is half a square.
figure.caption: The special triangles give exact ratios. Use the angle labels to identify the opposite and adjacent sides.

blocks.title: Use a known exact sine or cosine
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(6\sin 45^\circ\).
blocks.solution:
\(\sin 45^\circ=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\)

\(6\sin 45^\circ=6\times\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=3 \sqrt{2}\)

Answer \(3 \sqrt{2}\).
blocks.hint: Use the exact value before multiplying.

blocks.html: Rounded calculator values do not meet a request for an exact answer.

blocks.title: Find an exact tangent value
blocks.prompt: Find the exact value of \(7\tan 60^\circ\).
blocks.solution:
\(\tan 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}\)

\(7\tan 60^\circ=7 \sqrt{3}\)

Answer \(7 \sqrt{3}\).
blocks.hint: Use the exact ratio of the two legs, or its memorised value.

blocks.html: Keep equivalent surd forms such as \(\frac1{\sqrt2}\) and \(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\) exact.

sections.title: How do the special triangles give exact values?
sections.label: Use halves of a square or equilateral triangle
sections.intro: Half a square forms the two equal legs and the diagonal. Half an equilateral triangle of side 2 has hypotenuse 2, short leg 1 and longer leg \(\sqrt3\).

blocks.html: Use the opposite over adjacent for tangent. This produces \(\tan30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\), \(\tan45^\circ=1\) and \(\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3\).

blocks.title: Use two exact trig values in an expression
blocks.prompt: Calculate the exact value of \(11\sin 30^\circ-6\cos 30^\circ\).
blocks.hint: Substitute both exact values first. Combine like surds only.

blocks.html: Use the half-equilateral triangle for 30° and 60°. The half-square gives the distinct 45° ratios.

blocks.title: Use two exact trig values in an expression
blocks.prompt: Calculate the exact value of \(11\cos 45^\circ+2\sin 45^\circ\).
blocks.hint: Substitute both exact values first. Combine like surds only.

blocks.html: The tangent at 90° is undefined because its denominator would be zero.

blocks.html: If a side is known exactly, keep its factor with the square root and simplify only where allowed.

blocks.title: Find an exact side length
blocks.prompt:
Triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled at \(B\). \(AC=11\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(A=60^\circ\).

Find \(AB\) in exact form.
blocks.solution:
AC is the hypotenuse. Use cos for the adjacent leg.

\(AB=11\cos 60^\circ=\frac{11}{2}\)

Answer \(\frac{11}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: Keep the surd or fraction from the chosen ratio.

blocks.html: Only like surds combine by adding their coefficients.

blocks.title: Work backwards with an exact trig value
blocks.prompt: Find the value of \(a\) if \(a\cos 30^\circ=6 \sqrt{3}\). Give an exact answer.
blocks.hint: Divide by the exact cosine value.

igcse-0580-trigonometry-trig-graphs.description: Sketch, recognise and read the three trigonometric graphs from 0° to 360°.

sections.title: How can I sketch sine using five key points?
sections.label: Plot values before joining
sections.intro: Sine starts at zero and finishes at zero over a complete turn. Its smooth curve has a maximum and a minimum.

blocks.html: Plot the y-values \(0,1,0,-1,0\) at the x-values \(0^\circ,90^\circ,180^\circ,270^\circ,360^\circ\). Join with a smooth curve.

figure.alt: Sine starts at zero, peaks at 90 degrees, crosses zero at 180 degrees, reaches minus one at 270 degrees and ends at zero.
figure.caption: \(y=\sin x\) rises to 1, falls to −1 and returns to 0 in a full turn.

blocks.title: Read the sign of a trigonometric graph
blocks.prompt: For the graph \(y=\cos x\), state whether the point at \(x=330^\circ\) is above, on or below the x-axis.
blocks.solution:
Find the position of the curve at the given angle.

The vertical coordinate is positive.

Answer Above the x-axis.
blocks.hint: Use the position relative to the horizontal axis.

blocks.html: Mark the minimum at 270°, rather than at the midpoint of the interval.

blocks.title: Locate a key graph point
blocks.prompt: The curve \(y=\cos x\) has a point with \(x=270^\circ\). If its vertical coordinate is \(y\), find \(y+10\).
blocks.solution:
At this key angle, the graph has vertical coordinate \(0\).

\(y+10=0+10=10\)

Answer \(10\).
blocks.hint: Use a zero, maximum or minimum before doing the addition.

blocks.html: Write the angles in degrees and mark both endpoints on the sketch.

sections.title: How do I recognise cosine and its symmetry?
sections.label: Locate its midpoint and endpoints
sections.intro: Cosine starts and finishes at 1 and has a minimum at the middle of a full turn. Its graph has mirror symmetry around \(x=180^\circ\).

blocks.html: Plot \(1,0,-1,0,1\) at the same five key angles. A horizontal line at a given height may give two angles.

figure.alt: Cosine starts at one, crosses zero at 90 degrees, has a minimum at 180 degrees, crosses zero at 270 degrees and ends at one.
figure.caption: \(y=\cos x\) starts and ends at 1, with its minimum at \(180^\circ\).

blocks.title: Use a key point on a specified interval
blocks.prompt: On \(y=\sin x\), find the angle at which the graph crosses or meets the horizontal axis in the interval \(177^\circ\le x\le 184^\circ\).
blocks.solution:
At \(180^\circ\), the graph has vertical coordinate \(0\). This angle lies inside the given interval.

igcse-0580-trigonometry-sine-rule.description: Pair opposite sides and angles, choose valid inverse-sine solutions and recognise when two triangles fit.

sections.title: When do I use the sine rule?
sections.label: Match each side with its opposite angle
sections.intro: An opposite pair consists of a known side and its opposite angle. A second pair includes the unknown length or angle.

blocks.html: Use \(\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}\) for two opposite pairs. Use its reciprocal form when it makes the unknown angle easier to isolate.

figure.alt: Triangle ABC is not right-angled. Side a faces A, side b faces B, and side c faces C.
figure.caption: Lower-case side labels are paired with the opposite upper-case angles.

blocks.title: Use two opposite pairs to find a side
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=45^\circ\), \(B=98^\circ\) and \(a=13\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(b\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
Match each side with the angle opposite it.

\(\frac{b}{\sin 98^\circ}=\frac{13}{\sin 45^\circ}\)

\(b=\frac{13\sin 98^\circ}{\sin 45^\circ}\)

Answer \(18.2\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Pair the known side with the angle opposite it.

blocks.html: An angle at an endpoint of a side is not the angle opposite that side.

blocks.title: Use two opposite pairs to find a side
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=46^\circ\), \(B=105^\circ\) and \(a=13\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(c\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
\(C=180^\circ-46^\circ-105^\circ=29^\circ\)

Match each side with the angle opposite it.

\(\frac{c}{\sin 29^\circ}=\frac{13}{\sin 46^\circ}\)

\(c=\frac{13\sin 29^\circ}{\sin 46^\circ}\)

Answer \(8.76\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Find the missing angle first. Pair the known side with the angle opposite it.

blocks.html: If you know the other two angles, use the sum of 180° to find the next opposite pair.

sections.title: Why can there be two answers for an angle?
sections.label: Compare an angle with its supplement
sections.intro: Within a triangle, an acute angle and its obtuse supplement have the same sine. Two side lengths and a non-included angle can sometimes fit two triangles.

blocks.html: Find the calculator angle \(\alpha\) and test \(180^\circ-\alpha\). In either case, the known angle plus the candidate must be less than 180°.

figure.alt: Two triangles share a fixed angle at A, the side AC and equal-length sides from C to two possible positions of B.
figure.caption: Two positions of B can produce the same opposite-side data. Test their angle sums.

blocks.title: Find both triangles in the ambiguous case
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=24^\circ\), \(a=13\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=20\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find all possible values of \(B\), to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
\(\frac{\sin B}{20}=\frac{\sin 24^\circ}{13}\)

\(\sin B=\frac{20\sin 24^\circ}{13}\)

The sine value gives one acute angle and its supplement. Both candidates satisfy \(A+B<180^\circ\).

Solutions \(\{38.7^\circ, 141.3^\circ\}\).
blocks.hint: An obtuse angle can have the same sine as an acute angle. Check both against the triangle sum.

blocks.html: Inverse sine alone returns the acute angle for a sine strictly between 0 and 1. The obtuse candidate may also fit.

blocks.title: Choose the valid angle from the sine rule
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(B=60^\circ\), \(a=13\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=18\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
\(\frac{\sin A}{13}=\frac{\sin 60^\circ}{18}\)

\(\sin A=\frac{13\sin 60^\circ}{18}\)

Since a is shorter than b, A is smaller than B. The supplementary angle would be too large.

\(A=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{13\sin 60^\circ}{18}\right)\)

Answer \(38.7^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Check the triangle's angle sum and the order of its side lengths.

blocks.html: Reject an angle if it leaves the third angle zero or negative.

sections.title: How do I know whether the data can make a triangle?
sections.label: Check the sine and the size of each angle
sections.intro: An interior angle lies between 0° and 180°. Its sine is positive and at most 1.

blocks.html: If your calculated sine is greater than 1, there is no such triangle. If it is 1, the target angle is 90° and you still need a valid angle sum.

blocks.title: Choose the valid angle from the sine rule
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(B=129^\circ\), \(a=13\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=19\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
\(\frac{\sin A}{13}=\frac{\sin 129^\circ}{19}\)

\(\sin A=\frac{13\sin 129^\circ}{19}\)

B is obtuse, so the other angle must be acute.

\(A=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{13\sin 129^\circ}{19}\right)\)

Answer \(32.1^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Check the triangle's angle sum and the order of its side lengths.

blocks.html: The longer side is opposite the larger angle. Use this to rule out an implausible candidate.

How many triangles satisfy these data?
blocks.solution:
\(\sin B=\frac{29\sin 79^\circ}{13}\)

The calculated sine is greater than 1. No angle has this sine.

Answer No triangle.

examples.question:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(B=41^\circ\), \(a=10\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=16\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
solution: Since a is shorter than b, A is smaller than B. The supplementary angle would be too large.

examples.title: Choose the valid angle from the sine rule
examples.question:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(B=110^\circ\), \(a=11\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=18\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
solution: B is obtuse, so the other angle must be acute.

examples.title: Decide when the sine rule has no solution
examples.question:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=60^\circ\), \(a=11\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=22\,\mathrm{cm}\).

How many triangles satisfy these data?

  1. No triangle
  2. One acute triangle
  3. One obtuse triangle
  4. Two distinct triangles
solution: The calculated sine is greater than 1. No angle has this sine.

extraPractice.title: Use two opposite pairs to find a side
extraPractice.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=42^\circ\), \(B=109^\circ\) and \(a=17\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(b\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.solution:
Match each side with the angle opposite it.

\(\frac{b}{\sin 109^\circ}=\frac{17}{\sin 42^\circ}\)

\(b=\frac{17\sin 109^\circ}{\sin 42^\circ}\)

Answer \(24\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: Pair the known side with the angle opposite it.

extraPractice.title: Use two opposite pairs to find a side
extraPractice.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=43^\circ\), \(B=116^\circ\) and \(a=17\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(c\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.solution:
\(C=180^\circ-43^\circ-116^\circ=21^\circ\)

Match each side with the angle opposite it.

\(\frac{c}{\sin 21^\circ}=\frac{17}{\sin 43^\circ}\)

\(c=\frac{17\sin 21^\circ}{\sin 43^\circ}\)

Answer \(8.93\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: Find the missing angle first. Pair the known side with the angle opposite it.

extraPractice.title: Find both triangles in the ambiguous case
extraPractice.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=31^\circ\), \(a=17\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=23\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find all possible values of \(B\), to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
\(\frac{\sin B}{23}=\frac{\sin 31^\circ}{17}\)

\(\sin B=\frac{23\sin 31^\circ}{17}\)

The sine value gives one acute angle and its supplement. Both candidates satisfy \(A+B<180^\circ\).

Solutions \(\{44.2^\circ, 135.8^\circ\}\).
extraPractice.hint: An obtuse angle can have the same sine as an acute angle. Check both against the triangle sum.

extraPractice.title: Choose the valid angle from the sine rule
extraPractice.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(B=59^\circ\), \(a=17\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=23\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
\(\frac{\sin A}{17}=\frac{\sin 59^\circ}{23}\)

\(\sin A=\frac{17\sin 59^\circ}{23}\)

Since a is shorter than b, A is smaller than B. The supplementary angle would be too large.

\(A=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{17\sin 59^\circ}{23}\right)\)

Answer \(39.3^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Check the triangle's angle sum and the order of its side lengths.

extraPractice.title: Choose the valid angle from the sine rule
extraPractice.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(B=113^\circ\), \(a=17\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=24\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(A\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
\(\frac{\sin A}{17}=\frac{\sin 113^\circ}{24}\)

\(\sin A=\frac{17\sin 113^\circ}{24}\)

B is obtuse, so the other angle must be acute.

\(A=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{17\sin 113^\circ}{24}\right)\)

Answer \(40.7^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Check the triangle's angle sum and the order of its side lengths.

extraPractice.title: Decide when the sine rule has no solution
extraPractice.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(A=76^\circ\), \(a=18\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(b=36\,\mathrm{cm}\).

How many triangles satisfy these data?
extraPractice.solution:
\(\sin B=\frac{36\sin 76^\circ}{18}\)

The calculated sine is greater than 1. No angle has this sine.

Answer No triangle.
extraPractice.hint: Before using inverse sine, check whether the ratio is at most 1.

glossary.definition: A side and the angle on its other side of the triangle.
An angle that adds to the given angle to make 180°.
Given data permitting two different triangles.

revision.body:
Methods

Known informationMethod
Match each side with its opposite angleUse \(\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}\) for two opposite pairs. Use its reciprocal form when it makes the unknown angle easier to isolate.
Compare an angle with its supplementFind the calculator angle \(\alpha\) and test \(180^\circ-\alpha\). In either case, the known angle plus the candidate must be less than 180°.
Check the sine and the size of each angleIf your calculated sine is greater than 1, there is no such triangle. If it is 1, the target angle is 90° and you still need a valid angle sum.

Worked line

\(\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}\)

Check yourself

If inverse sine gives \(49^\circ\) for B and \(A=38^\circ\), what are the two possible values of B?

Answer \(49^\circ,\ 131^\circ\)
revision.checks:
• An angle at an endpoint of a side is not the angle opposite that side.
  • Inverse sine alone returns the acute angle for a sine strictly between 0 and 1. The obtuse candidate may also fit.
  • The longer side is opposite the larger angle. Use this to rule out an implausible candidate.
revision.examTip: State the reason when an obtuse or acute solution is excluded.

igcse-0580-trigonometry-cosine-rule-and-.description: Choose the cosine rule or area formula when given two sides and their included angle, or three sides.

sections.title: Which formula finds a side from two sides and an angle?
sections.label: Choose the included angle
sections.intro: With known sides a and b and the angle C between them, the cosine rule determines the opposite side c.

blocks.html: Calculate \(c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C\), then take the positive square root.

figure.alt: The angle at C lies between side lengths a and b. Side c is opposite C.
figure.caption: Use the marked included angle with sides a and b for the area formula or the cosine rule.

blocks.title: Find a side with the cosine rule
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(a=9\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(b=8\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(C=63^\circ\).

Find \(c\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
C is the included angle between a and b.

\(c^2=9^2+8^2-2\times9\times8\cos 63^\circ\)

Take the positive square root.

Answer \(8.92\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: The given angle must be between the known sides.

blocks.html: An angle at the wrong vertex does not fit the formula with those sides.

blocks.title: Choose the rule for two sides and an included angle
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(a=10\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(b=8\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(C=64^\circ\).

Which method can find \(c\) in one step?
blocks.solution:
There is no complete opposite pair and the angle is not 90В°. Two sides and their included angle determine a third side by the cosine rule.

Answer Cosine rule.
blocks.hint: Look for the known included angle and no complete opposite pair.

blocks.html: An obtuse C has negative cosine. The final term then increases the square of c.

sections.title: How do I use three lengths to find an angle?
sections.label: Rearrange for cosine first
sections.intro: All three sides determine a triangle if the sum of each pair exceeds the remaining side.

blocks.html: For the angle opposite c use \(\cos C=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\). Then use inverse cosine.

blocks.title: Find an angle from all three sides
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(a=3\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(b=9\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(c=11\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(C\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
C is opposite c, so the squared length of c is subtracted in the numerator.

\(\cos C=\frac{3^2+9^2-11^2}{54}\)

\(C=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{3^2+9^2-11^2}{54}\right)\)

Answer \(125.0^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Use the rearranged cosine rule. A negative cosine is consistent with an obtuse angle.

blocks.html: Subtract the square of the side opposite the target angle, rather than the side closest to it.

blocks.title: Find an angle from all three sides
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(a=7\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(b=16\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(c=22\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find \(C\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
C is opposite c, so the squared length of c is subtracted in the numerator.

\(\cos C=\frac{7^2+16^2-22^2}{224}\)

\(C=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{7^2+16^2-22^2}{224}\right)\)

Answer \(143.0^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Use the rearranged cosine rule. A negative cosine is consistent with an obtuse angle.

blocks.html: Check that the largest angle faces the longest side.

sections.title: What if the question asks for area or supplies it?
sections.label: Use the sine of the included angle
sections.intro: Two known sides can enclose an acute, right or obtuse angle. Their area always uses the positive sine of the angle between them.

blocks.html: Use \(\text{Area}=\frac12 ab\sin C\). If the area is given, rearrange for the missing side or for the sine of C.

Known informationMethod
Two perpendicular sidesPythagoras or a right-angled ratio depending on the target.
A known opposite pairTry the sine rule.
Two sides and the included angleCosine rule for the third side. Use the triangle area formula for area.
Three sidesUse the cosine rule rearranged for the angle you need.

blocks.title: Find area from two sides and the included angle
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(a=5\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(b=9\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(C=67^\circ\).

Find the area to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
Use the sine of the angle between the given sides.

\(\mathcal A=\frac{1}{2}\times5\times9\sin 67^\circ\)

Answer \(20.7\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Use the included angle and keep the factor of one half.

blocks.html: When finding an angle from its sine, the named acute or obtuse condition tells you which supplement to keep.

blocks.title: Recover a side from the area
blocks.prompt:
In triangle \(ABC\), \(a=12\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(C=69^\circ\).

Its area is \(54\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}\). Find \(b\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
\(54=\frac{1}{2}\times 12\times b\sin 69^\circ\)

\(b=\frac{108}{12\sin 69^\circ}\)

Answer \(9.64\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Multiply the area by two before dividing.

blocks.html: Distinguish the cosine rule for a length from the sine calculation for the area.

\(b=\frac{168}{14\sin 98^\circ}\)

extraPractice.title: Find the obtuse included angle from area
extraPractice.prompt:

The area is \(\frac{621}{20}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}\). Angle \(C\) is obtuse. Find \(C\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
\(\sin C=\frac{\frac{621}{10}}{207}=\frac{3}{10}\)

Use the supplement of the acute calculator result.

\(C=180^\circ-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)\)

Answer \(162.5^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.

igcse-0580-trigonometry-three-dimensiona.description: Find a space diagonal and use a projection to measure the angle between a line and a plane.

sections.title: Which right triangle should I use first?
sections.label: Start in the base plane
sections.intro: Choose the base plane. Project the endpoint vertically onto it. In a cuboid, the projection of a space diagonal is a diagonal of the base.

blocks.html: Find the base diagonal using Pythagoras. It forms a right triangle with the vertical height and the space diagonal.

figure.alt: A cuboid shows a diagonal from A on the base to G above the base point C. The highlighted right triangle contains AC, CG and AG.
figure.caption: AC is the projection of the diagonal AG on the base plane. The required angle is between AC and AG.

blocks.title: Find the horizontal projection
blocks.prompt:
A cuboid has base edges \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\), and height \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find the exact distance between opposite vertices on its base.
blocks.solution:
Only the two horizontal edges enter the base diagonal.

\(d^2=10^2+8^2\)

\(d=\sqrt{164}\)

Answer \(2 \sqrt{41}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: Work in the base rectangle first.

blocks.html: Using an edge of the base would give the diagonal of a side face and omit one dimension.

blocks.title: Find a cuboid space diagonal
blocks.prompt:
A cuboid has base edges \(11\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\), and height \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Calculate the exact length of a space diagonal.
blocks.solution:
Find the base diagonal first.

\(d=\sqrt{185}\)

The vertical edge is perpendicular to the base diagonal.

\(D^2=185+4^2\)

\(D=\sqrt{201}\)

Answer \(\sqrt{201}\,\mathrm{cm}\).
blocks.hint: Use the base diagonal and then the perpendicular height.

blocks.html: Draw a clean two-dimensional triangle before substituting values.

sections.title: How do I find the angle between a line and a plane?
sections.label: Measure from the projected line
sections.intro: The line and its projection meet at a point in the plane. Their angle is the angle between the line and the plane.

blocks.html: Use inverse tangent of the vertical rise divided by the projection length.

blocks.title: Find the angle of a line with its base plane
blocks.prompt:
A cuboid has base edges \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\), and height \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find the acute angle between a space diagonal and the base plane, to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
Project the upper endpoint vertically down to the base. The projected line is the base diagonal.

\(d=\sqrt{97}\)

\(\tan \theta=\frac{5}{\sqrt{97}}\)

\(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt{97}}\right)\)

Answer \(26.9^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Compare the space diagonal with its projection on the base, not with a base edge.

blocks.html: An angle with the vertical edge is measured at the other end of the space diagonal. It is the complement of the angle with the base.

blocks.title: Distinguish the angle with a vertical edge
blocks.prompt:
A cuboid has base edges \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\), and height \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Find the acute angle between a space diagonal and the vertical edge at the same upper vertex, to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
\(d=\sqrt{106}\)

The given angle is at the upper vertex. The opposite leg is the base diagonal.

\(\tan \phi=\frac{\sqrt{106}}{6}\)

\(\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{106}}{6}\right)\)

Answer \(59.8^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Mark the angle at the upper vertex between the diagonal and the vertical.

blocks.html: Point out the projection when you name the angle in your working.

sections.title: What is the projection of an edge in a pyramid?
sections.label: Use the correct point in the base
sections.intro: In a right square-based pyramid, the perpendicular from the apex meets the centre of the square base.

blocks.html: The projection of an apex-to-corner edge runs from the centre to a corner. It has length half a base diagonal.

figure.alt: A square-based pyramid has apex T above the base centre O. A segment from O to vertex A is half the base diagonal.
figure.caption: Project the edge TA on the base. The projected segment ends at the centre O.

blocks.title: Recover the vertical height
blocks.prompt: A cuboid has base edges \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\). Its space diagonal makes an angle of \(39^\circ\) with the base plane. Find the vertical height to 3 significant figures.
blocks.solution:
\(d=\sqrt{117}\)

The vertical height is opposite the base angle.

\(h=\sqrt{117}\tan 39^\circ\)

Answer \(8.76\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Use the base diagonal as the adjacent leg.

blocks.html: For a sloping face height the projection would end at an edge midpoint, not at a corner.

blocks.title: Project an edge of a square-based pyramid
blocks.prompt: A right square-based pyramid has base edge \(13\,\mathrm{cm}\) and vertical height \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the angle between an apex-to-corner edge and the base plane, to 1 decimal place.
blocks.solution:
The apex projects to the centre of the base. The projection runs from the centre to a corner.

\(d=\frac{\sqrt{338}}{2}=\frac{13 \sqrt{2}}{2}\)

\(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{\frac{13 \sqrt{2}}{2}}\right)\)

Answer \(33.1^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
blocks.hint: Use half the base diagonal. Half a base side would project a face slant height.

blocks.html: Separate an apex-to-corner edge from the line down a triangular face.

The given angle is at the upper vertex. The opposite leg is the base diagonal.

\(\tan \phi=\frac{\sqrt{244}}{13}\)

\(\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{244}}{13}\right)\)

Answer \(50.2^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Mark the angle at the upper vertex between the diagonal and the vertical.

extraPractice.title: Recover the vertical height
extraPractice.prompt: A cuboid has base edges \(11\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\). Its space diagonal makes an angle of \(32^\circ\) with the base plane. Find the vertical height to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.solution:
\(d=\sqrt{265}\)

The vertical height is opposite the base angle.

\(h=\sqrt{265}\tan 32^\circ\)

Answer \(10.2\,\mathrm{cm}\) to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: Use the base diagonal as the adjacent leg.

extraPractice.title: Project an edge of a square-based pyramid
extraPractice.prompt: A right square-based pyramid has base edge \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\) and vertical height \(9\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the angle between an apex-to-corner edge and the base plane, to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.solution:
The apex projects to the centre of the base. The projection runs from the centre to a corner.

\(d=\frac{\sqrt{288}}{2}=6 \sqrt{2}\)

\(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{9}{6 \sqrt{2}}\right)\)

Answer \(46.7^\circ\) to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Use half the base diagonal. Half a base side would project a face slant height.
